cards.front: How are dietary supplements regulated in the USA under DSHEA (1994)?
cards.back: Herbal (botanical) products, vitamins, minerals, amino acids and similar products are legally dietary supplements, regulated as foods rather than drugs. Manufacturers need not prove efficacy or safety before marketing (only a new dietary ingredient needs some safety data); the FDA must prove harm before removing or restricting a product. Labels carry structure-function claims.

cards.front: What quality problems affect herbal supplements?
cards.back: GMP standards required by DSHEA were finalised only in 2007, so manufacturers long self-regulated: plant misidentification and species substitution (DNA barcoding found substitution in about a third of samples), adulteration with pharmaceuticals, contamination, and variable potency. Since 2006, manufacturers must report serious adverse events to the FDA.

cards.front: Why is 'natural' not the same as safe? List the hazards of herbal products.
cards.back: Botanicals may be inert or intrinsically toxic; products may be misidentified, adulterated or contaminated; they are rarely tested for dose-response, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity or teratogenicity; adverse effects are under-reported and seldom chemically analysed; and their many constituents make drug-interaction testing difficult. Placebo effects (30-50% of response) also confound efficacy claims.

cards.front: Which quality practices does WHO advise for herbal medicines?
cards.back: Good Agricultural and Collection Practice (GACP) at cultivation, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) from crude powder or extract to purified product, and Good Supply Practice (GSP) during marketing. Traditional medicines generally lack controlled trials and documented safety and efficacy data.

cards.front: What is a phytopharmaceutical drug under India's New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019?
cards.back: A new-drug category: a purified, standardised fraction of a medicinal plant extract with at least four defined bioactive or phytochemical compounds, assessed qualitatively and quantitatively, for internal or external (not parenteral) use. It must show quality, safety and efficacy and is distinct from Ayurvedic, Unani or Siddha medicines.

cards.front: Complete: herbal products to avoid and their toxicity
cards.text: Aristolochia (aristolochic acid): {{nephrotoxicity}} and cancer. Comfrey, borage and coltsfoot: {{pyrrolizidine alkaloid}} hepatotoxicity. Ephedra (ma-huang): {{CNS and cardiac}} toxicity. Kava-kava, chaparral and germander: {{hepatotoxicity}}. Pennyroyal: liver and {{renal failure}}. Aconite: alkaloid {{cardiac}} and CNS effects. Kratom: {{dependence}}, respiratory depression, seizures.

cards.front: How can traditional remedies cause heavy metal or stimulant toxicity?
cards.back: Some folk medicines, including certain Ayurvedic preparations, and kohl cosmetics contain lead; skin-lightening creams and folk remedies may contain mercury. 'Fat burner' supplements may contain caffeine, and the herb ma-huang contains ephedrine, which can cause stimulant toxicity.

cards.front: Short note: St. John's wort (Hypericum)

points: Hypericin (standardisation marker) and hyperforin; several compounds probably act together
Extract inhibits reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine (hyperforin)
Better than placebo and comparable to SSRIs in mild to moderate depression, with fewer side effects; onset 2-4 weeks
Photosensitisation (hypericin): sunscreen and eye protection
GI upset, fatigue, dizziness; hypomania or mania
Serotonin syndrome with antidepressants and stimulants

Hyperforin activates PXR, inducing CYP3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: subtherapeutic digoxin, oral contraceptives (pregnancy), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, HIV protease inhibitors and NNRTIs, warfarin, rivaroxaban, irinotecan, theophylline, anticonvulsants

cards.front: Garlic supplement: active principle, claimed effects and interactions.
cards.back: Alliin is converted by alliinase to allicin (the odour principle); enteric coating protects the enzyme from gastric acid. Claimed effects: modest lipid lowering (allicin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase in vitro), antiplatelet and fibrinolytic action, antimicrobial activity. Adverse: GI upset, breath and body odour, hypotension, rare bleeding. Use cautiously with anticoagulants and antiplatelets (including ibuprofen); may lower saquinavir levels.

cards.front: Ginkgo biloba: claimed uses, evidence and safety concerns.
cards.back: Leaf extract (flavone glycosides, ginkgolides, bilobalide) increases blood flow, antagonises platelet-activating factor and scavenges free radicals. Promoted for dementia and claudication, but trial benefits are inconsistent and unlikely to be clinically relevant. Risks: bleeding with aspirin or warfarin, so avoid with antiplatelets or anticoagulants; seizures from ginkgotoxin in seed contamination, so avoid in epilepsy.

cards.front: Which drug interactions have been reported with ginkgo in case reports?
cards.back: Virologic failure with efavirenz, sedation with trazodone, priapism with risperidone, seizures with valproate and phenytoin, and mood dysregulation in schizophrenia; all need confirmation by pharmacokinetic studies.

cards.front: Ginseng: active principles, uses and precautions.
cards.back: Panax species contain ginsenosides (Siberian ginseng is a different plant with eleutherosides). Promoted as an adaptogen; best evidence is modest lowering of fasting glucose and possible cold prevention. Adverse: insomnia, nervousness, mania, hypertension, oestrogen-like effects (mastalgia, vaginal bleeding). Interactions: mania with phenelzine, lithium or neuroleptics; antiplatelet effect, so avoid with anticoagulants and around surgery; caution with hypoglycaemic drugs.

cards.front: Echinacea: use, evidence and precautions.
cards.back: Used for colds and respiratory infections as an immune modulator. A Cochrane review found no significant benefit in treating colds overall, at most a small preventive effect. Adverse: unpleasant taste, GI upset, allergic rash (more in children). Avoid in immune deficiency (e.g. AIDS, cancer) and autoimmune disease until its immune effects are clarified.

cards.front: Milk thistle: constituent, use and safety.
cards.back: Silymarin (mainly silybin) from fruit and seeds; poor oral bioavailability. Claimed hepatoprotection via antioxidant, free-radical scavenging, glutathione-raising and anti-inflammatory (NF-kB) actions; clinical evidence in liver disease is insufficient. Adverse effects are rare (laxative at high doses), and it poses no meaningful drug-interaction risk.

cards.front: Saw palmetto: use and pharmacology.
cards.back: Promoted for benign prostatic hyperplasia. In vitro it inhibits 5-alpha-reductase I and II, blocks DHT binding and alpha-1 receptors, but human effects on DHT are inconsistent. Generic extracts showed no benefit, while a hexane extract improved nocturia and flow. It does not lower PSA, so it does not interfere with prostate cancer screening; side effects are mild and fewer sexual effects than tamsulosin or finasteride are claimed.

cards.front: Complete: supplements that alter bleeding risk
cards.text: Antiplatelet effect, so caution with anticoagulants and NSAIDs: {{garlic}}, {{ginkgo}} and {{ginseng}}. {{Glucosamine}} may raise the INR on warfarin. Reduce warfarin effect: {{coenzyme Q10}} (structurally like vitamin K), {{St. John's wort}} (enzyme induction) and possibly melatonin.

cards.front: Coenzyme Q10: claimed uses, evidence and interaction.
cards.back: A mitochondrial antioxidant (ubiquinone). Evidence: small BP reductions, modest improvement in heart failure outcomes and ejection fraction, uncertain benefit in ischaemic heart disease; it did not reduce statin-induced myopathy in meta-analysis (statins lower its synthesis). Well tolerated. Because it resembles vitamin K, it may reduce warfarin effect.

cards.front: Glucosamine: use, formulation issue and precautions.
cards.back: Cartilage substrate used for knee osteoarthritis. The sulfate (especially crystalline) form may help pain and joint-space narrowing; the hydrochloride form is ineffective, which explains conflicting trials. It has no direct analgesic effect and benefit takes 1-2 months. Mild GI effects; possible shellfish cross-allergy; may raise INR with warfarin.

cards.front: Melatonin supplement: uses, adverse effects and interactions.
cards.back: Pineal hormone regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Used for jet lag (best taken at target bedtime, more effective eastbound and across 5 or more time zones), insomnia and pre-operative anxiety; it inspired the receptor agonist ramelteon. Adverse: next-day drowsiness, headache, BP changes; may lower prolactin, so avoid in nursing. Metabolised by CYP1A2 (fluvoxamine interaction); may reduce warfarin effect; interacts with nifedipine.

cards.front: What is reverse pharmacology?
cards.back: Drug discovery that runs 'clinics to laboratory': documented clinical experience with traditional (e.g. Ayurvedic) remedies is the starting point, followed by experimental validation of activity and targets. It is cheaper and faster with a higher success rate than random screening, and relies on a 'golden triangle' of traditional knowledge, modern medicine and modern science.

cards.front: Give Indian examples of drugs developed from Ayurvedic leads.
cards.back: Rauwolfia serpentina: antihypertensive and tranquillising effects shown by Gananath Sen and Kartik Bose (1931). Guggulipid from Commiphora mukul: hypolipidaemic, approved by DCGI in 1986. Bacopa monnieri (Brahmi): memory enhancer developed by CDRI Lucknow. Sir Ram Nath Chopra and Gananath Sen introduced reverse pharmacology of Ayurvedic drugs in India.

cards.front: Complete: Ayurvedic plant sources and their uses
cards.text: Rauwolfia serpentina (sarpagandha): {{hypertension}}. Withania somnifera (ashwagandha): {{anti-stress and immunomodulatory}}. Commiphora mukul (guggul): {{hypolipidaemic}}. Curcuma longa (turmeric): {{anti-inflammatory}}. Mucuna pruriens: {{parkinsonism}}. Psoralea corylifolia (babchi): {{vitiligo and psoriasis}}. Black pepper piperidines: {{bioavailability enhancers}}. Bacopa monnieri (brahmi): {{memory enhancer}}.

cards.front: What role can physicians play in ethnopharmacology?
cards.back: Field work documenting patients who use herbal remedies and the diseases treated; clinical studies of herbs to identify drug candidates; and comparing benefit and harm of herbal, modern and combined therapy in patients who take both.

cards.front: Essay: Dietary supplements and herbal medicines: regulation, safety and interactions

points: Widespread use; legally foods in the USA, not drugs
Distinguish from plant-derived prescription drugs (morphine, digitalis, atropine)
DSHEA 1994: no pre-marketing proof of efficacy or safety
GMP, adverse event reporting
WHO GACP, GMP, GSP; India: phytopharmaceutical category (2019 rules)
St. John's wort, garlic, ginkgo, ginseng, echinacea, milk thistle, saw palmetto
Coenzyme Q10, glucosamine, melatonin
Intrinsically toxic herbs (aristolochia, comfrey, kava, ephedra)
Adulteration, contamination, heavy metals
St. John's wort induction via PXR; serotonin syndrome
Bleeding with garlic, ginkgo, ginseng; warfarin changes with CoQ10, glucosamine
Ask about supplement use non-judgementally
Use evidence-based sources; report adverse events
